candidates.whyNotable: Endlessly quoted in sermons and Christian apologetics, but Wikiquote finds no source in Gandhi's works; a very similar line is attributed to 'Bara Dada' in E. Stanley Jones's The Christ of the Indian Road (1925).

candidates.quote: I think it would be a good idea.
candidates.trueOrigin: Apocryphal; earliest located attribution is a 1967 CBS News documentary 'The Italians' (per Reader's Digest 1967), popularized via E. F. Schumacher's Good Work (1979).
candidates.whyNotable: The famous quip supposedly given when Gandhi was asked what he thought of Western civilization; QI shows the earliest source is a 1967 CBS documentary nearly 20 years after his death, with no film or biographical record of him saying it.

candidates.quote: He who lives in harmony with himself lives in harmony with the universe.
candidates.trueOrigin: Appears in Dan Millman's 1995 'The Life You Were Born to Live'; no confirmed Meditations source, likely a modern paraphrase.
candidates.whyNotable: Frequently shared as Stoic wisdom, but Wikiquote lists it as unverified - it surfaces in Dan Millman's 1995 self-help book with no confirmed source in the Meditations.

candidates.quote: But suppose the child inherited my beauty and your brains?
candidates.trueOrigin: A floating joke that predates Monroe by decades, told earlier about George Bernard Shaw, Isadora Duncan, and others.
candidates.whyNotable: The famous 'beauty and brains' comeback (often set as a Monroe-and-Einstein or Monroe-and-Bernard-Shaw exchange); QI shows the joke circulated long before Monroe and is a floating anecdote.

candidates.quote: There are three kinds of lies: lies, damned lies, and statistics.
candidates.trueOrigin: Twain attributed it to Benjamin Disraeli; actual coiner is unconfirmed (various late-19th-century candidates).
candidates.whyNotable: Twain popularized and helped spread this line but himself credited it to Benjamin Disraeli; the true originator remains disputed.

candidates.quote: The old law of an eye for an eye leaves everybody blind.
candidates.trueOrigin: Proverb of indefinite origin, variously attributed to Gandhi and others; no verified King source.
candidates.whyNotable: Widely credited to King (and used in Spike Lee's 'Do the Right Thing') but the underlying 'eye for an eye leaves everybody blind' proverb has no firm origin and is also pinned on Gandhi.

candidates.quote: To be a Christian without prayer is no more possible than to be alive without breathing.
candidates.trueOrigin: First attributed to King by George Sweeting (Moody Church) in 1979; no earlier documentation.
candidates.whyNotable: Frequently shared as King, but Wikiquote finds no source earlier than pastor George Sweeting's 1979 book, casting doubt on the attribution.

candidates.quote: Poetry is music written for the human voice.
candidates.trueOrigin: Angelou attributed it to her mentor Bertha Flowers, not to herself.
candidates.whyNotable: Frequently attributed to Angelou, but she herself credited the expression to her mentor Bertha Flowers, so the popular attribution is a reassignment.

candidates.quote: There is not a single citizen in South Africa who is not ready to stand by his Palestinian brothers in their legitimate fight against the Zionist racists.
candidates.trueOrigin: Circulated via Mathaba.net with no verified primary source; Wikiquote lists it as disputed and the wording does not match any authenticated Mandela statement.
candidates.whyNotable: The sole entry in Wikiquote's Disputed section for Mandela; politically charged and lacks a verified source, so flag for editorial judgment before building.

candidates.quote: A pessimist is one who, when he has the choice of two evils, chooses both.
candidates.trueOrigin: Unattributed until 1977; similar formulations appear from 1899 onward with no link to Wilde.
candidates.whyNotable: Widely shared definition of a pessimist credited to Wilde, but Wikiquote finds no attribution to him until 1977.

candidates.quote: I don't want to go to heaven. None of my friends are there.
candidates.trueOrigin: No known source in Wilde's writings; Wikiquote notes the attribution circulating via Goodreads-era social sharing with no citation.
candidates.whyNotable: Popular irreverent one-liner with no documented Wilde source; a classic quote-card fabrication.

candidates.quote: I have nothing to declare except my genius.
candidates.trueOrigin: Apocryphal customs anecdote; QI notes the earliest citation is 1910, nearly two decades after the supposed 1882 incident and a decade after Wilde's death.
candidates.whyNotable: The iconic 'customs official' quip; QI rates the evidence weak because it first surfaces long after the event and after Wilde had died.

candidates.quote: Some cause happiness wherever they go; others whenever they go.
candidates.trueOrigin: Anonymous; QI finds it in an insurance magazine (1908) and traces the Wilde attribution to a possible misreading of a 1947 aphorism collection.
candidates.whyNotable: Beloved back-handed insult attributed to Wilde; QI finds no evidence he ever used it and pins the earliest instance to an anonymous 1908 source.

candidates.quote: True friends stab you in the front.
candidates.trueOrigin: No Wilde source; earliest instances tied to Walter Winchell (1955) and others; Wilde attribution only began circa 1989.
candidates.whyNotable: Edgy friendship aphorism commonly tagged Wilde; Wikiquote finds no source before the mid-20th century, long after his death.

candidates.quote: I do not seek. I find.
candidates.trueOrigin: Spanish 'Yo no busco, yo encuentro'; quoted in Graham Sutherland's 1936 essay 'A Trend in English Draughtsmanship' but the direct attribution to Picasso is disputed.
candidates.whyNotable: A famous aphoristic Picasso line whose earliest sighting is a 1936 essay by Graham Sutherland, with Wikiquote flagging the direct attribution as disputed.

candidates.quote: Inspiration exists, but it has to find you working.
candidates.trueOrigin: Attributed to Picasso only in a 1994 publication (Spanish: 'La inspiración existe, pero tiene que encontrarte trabajando'); no contemporaneous source in Picasso's own words is documented.
candidates.whyNotable: A studio-motivation staple credited to Picasso, but the earliest documented attribution is a 1994 posthumous source with no primary record.

candidates.quote: It took me four years to paint like Raphael, but a lifetime to paint like a child.
candidates.trueOrigin: Only appears in print from 1998, posthumously; multiple variant wordings exist ('At eight I was Raphael...') and no contemporaneous primary source is documented.
candidates.whyNotable: A hugely popular Picasso maxim that surfaces only in posthumous 1998 sources with shifting wording, so Wikiquote treats it as unverified.

candidates.quote: Successful people never worry about what others are doing.
candidates.trueOrigin: No source in any of Plato's works; earliest occurrence is a 2011 tweet.
candidates.whyNotable: A modern motivational-meme line credited to Plato that Wikiquote traces only to a 2011 tweet.

candidates.quote: The highest form of pure thought is in mathematics.
candidates.trueOrigin: No source in Plato's writings; earliest example found on Google Books is a 1990 Usenet post.
candidates.whyNotable: A commonly-quoted 'Plato' line on math and reason that Wikiquote can trace no earlier than a 1990 Usenet post.

candidates.quote: Wise men speak because they have something to say; fools because they have to say something.
candidates.trueOrigin: Cannot be found complete in Plato's writings; likely a conflation of passages from the Symposium and Laches.
candidates.whyNotable: An extremely popular 'Plato' aphorism Wikiquote flags as unverifiable, likely stitched together from separate dialogues.

candidates.quote: The problem is not that people are taxed too little, the problem is that government spends too much.
candidates.trueOrigin: Listed by Wikiquote as merely attributed; earliest sourcing points to Richard A. Viguerie's book 'Conservatives Betrayed' (p. 43) rather than a primary Reagan speech.
candidates.whyNotable: Endlessly reproduced as a Reagan tax quote, yet Wikiquote can only source it to a secondary book, not to Reagan himself.

candidates.quote: And those who were seen dancing were thought to be insane by those who could not hear the music.
candidates.trueOrigin: Anonymous/proverbial; earliest precursor Anne Louise Germaine de Staël, De l'Allemagne (1813); modern phrasing popularized by George Carlin's Brain Droppings (1997), later credited by him to 'Anon.' Not from Rumi or Nietzsche.
candidates.whyNotable: Massively shared, credited to both Rumi and Nietzsche; QI finds no evidence for either and calls it anonymous, with a Germaine de Staël precursor (1813) and George Carlin popularizing the modern wording in 1997.

candidates.quote: Everyone has been made for some particular work, and the desire for that work has been put in every heart.
candidates.trueOrigin: No primary Rumi source established; earliest citation is a modern secondary work (Jan Phillips, Marry Your Muse, 1997).
candidates.whyNotable: A common graduation- and career-inspiration 'Rumi' line, but Wikiquote can source it only to a 1997 creativity self-help book (Jan Phillips, Marry Your Muse), not to Rumi's works.

candidates.quote: Let the beauty of what you love be what you do.
candidates.trueOrigin: No primary Rumi source established; earliest citation is a modern secondary compilation (Linda J. Ferguson, Path for Greatness: Spirituality at Work, 2000).
candidates.whyNotable: One of the most-shared 'Rumi' lines on social media and tattoos, but Wikiquote can source it only to a 2000 self-help book (Linda J. Ferguson, Path for Greatness), not to any of Rumi's actual works.

candidates.quote: We are all broken. That's how the light gets in.
candidates.trueOrigin: No single author; a modern paraphrase-blend of Ernest Hemingway (A Farewell to Arms, 1929) and Leonard Cohen ('Anthem', 1992), with conceptual precursors in Emerson (1841) and Benjamin Blood (1860). Not from Rumi.
candidates.whyNotable: A viral inspirational line pinned variously on Rumi, Hemingway, and Leonard Cohen; QI finds no real source and traces it to a 2013-era social-media blend of Hemingway's 1929 'the world breaks everyone' and Cohen's 1992 'there is a crack in everything, that's how the light gets in.'

candidates.quote: Wherever you stand, be the soul of that place.
candidates.trueOrigin: No primary Rumi source established; earliest citation is a modern secondary work (Patricia Flasch, Becoming a Love Dog, 2009).
candidates.whyNotable: A widely reposted 'Rumi' aphorism whose only citation on Wikiquote is a 2009 book (Patricia Flasch, Becoming a Love Dog), not any verified Rumi text.

candidates.quote: You were born with wings. Why prefer to crawl through life?
candidates.trueOrigin: No primary Rumi source established; earliest citation is a modern compilation (Larry Chang, Wisdom for the Soul, 2006).
candidates.whyNotable: A ubiquitous feel-good 'Rumi' quote across Instagram and posters, but Wikiquote traces it only to a 2006 quotation anthology (Larry Chang, Wisdom for the Soul), with no link to Rumi's documented writings.

candidates.quote: Build your opponent a golden bridge to retreat across.
candidates.trueOrigin: A paraphrase blending Sun Tzu's 'leave a way of escape' with later commentary (Tu Mu); the 'golden bridge' phrasing is not in Sun Tzu's own words.
candidates.whyNotable: A vivid maxim credited to Sun Tzu that Wikiquote lists as disputed — it dresses up his 'leave an outlet' principle in words he never wrote.

candidates.quote: Victory is reserved for those who are willing to pay its price.
candidates.trueOrigin: Does not appear in The Art of War; Wikiquote lists it as disputed with no located source, possibly a modern/anime misattribution.
candidates.whyNotable: A heavily-shared 'Sun Tzu' motivational line Wikiquote flags as disputed and unlocated in any translation.

candidates.quote: A man who has never gone to school may steal from a freight car; but if he has a university education, he may steal the whole railroad.
candidates.trueOrigin: Unverified; earliest citation is a 1952 book (William Joseph Grace, 'Art of Communicating Ideas'), decades after Roosevelt's death, with no contemporaneous source.
candidates.whyNotable: A widely-circulated zinger about education and corruption credited to TR; Wikiquote lists it as disputed with only a much-later 1952 secondhand citation and no Roosevelt primary source.

candidates.quote: A thorough knowledge of the Bible is worth more than a college education.
candidates.trueOrigin: Unverified; earliest citation is 'Stepping Stones: The Complete Bible Narratives' (1941), with no contemporaneous Roosevelt source.
candidates.whyNotable: A frequently-shared line in religious and inspirational contexts attributed to TR; Wikiquote flags it as disputed, with only a 1941 secondhand quotation and no Roosevelt primary source.

candidates.quote: When they call the roll in the Senate, the Senators do not know whether to answer 'Present' or 'Not Guilty'.
candidates.trueOrigin: Unverified; no primary source ties the line to Roosevelt, and Wikiquote carries it without any sourced citation.
candidates.whyNotable: A recurring political-corruption quip attributed to TR; Wikiquote lists it as disputed with no reliable source establishing Roosevelt as the author.

candidates.quote: I have recently been examining all the known superstitions of the world, and do not find in our particular superstition one redeeming feature.
candidates.trueOrigin: Unverified; sourced only to an unlocated letter cited by John E. Remsburg (Six Historic Americans, 1906); Monticello scholars consider it unreliable
candidates.whyNotable: A favorite anti-religion Jefferson quote; Wikiquote and the Jefferson Foundation deem it spurious — it rests on an unlocated "letter to Dr. Woods" cited by John Remsburg in 1906 that no one has ever verified.

candidates.quote: Doctors are men who prescribe medicines of which they know little, to cure diseases of which they know less, in human beings of whom they know nothing
candidates.trueOrigin: No verified Voltaire source; earliest appearances circa 1956
candidates.whyNotable: A much-shared cynical medical quip; Wikiquote notes it only surfaces in publications from 1956 onward with no original French source ever located in Voltaire.

candidates.quote: Etymology is a science in which the vowels count for nothing, and the consonants for very little
candidates.trueOrigin: No verified Voltaire source; earliest link is A. W. von Schlegel's 1815 review
candidates.whyNotable: A witty line about linguistics attributed to Voltaire since an 1815 Schlegel review, but neither Wikiquote nor QI can find it anywhere in Voltaire's own writings.

candidates.quote: Men occasionally stumble over the truth, but most of them pick themselves up and hurry off as if nothing had happened
candidates.trueOrigin: Unverified; earliest evidence Reader's Digest (April 1942), authorship unclear (QI).
candidates.whyNotable: Widely credited to Churchill, but Quote Investigator finds the earliest 1942 Reader's Digest instance and notes the barb was reportedly aimed at Churchill's rival Stanley Baldwin, not spoken by him.

candidates.quote: Never let a good crisis go to waste
candidates.trueOrigin: Popularized by Rahm Emanuel (2008); concept from Saul Alinsky's Rules for Radicals (1971). Not Churchill.
candidates.whyNotable: Frequently pinned on Churchill but popularized by Rahm Emanuel in 2008 and rooted in Saul Alinsky's 1971 Rules for Radicals, with no Churchill source.

candidates.quote: This is the sort of bloody nonsense up with which I will not put
candidates.trueOrigin: Anonymous anecdote; earliest 1942 Strand Magazine version credits an unnamed English master, not Churchill (QI).
candidates.whyNotable: The famous 'don't end a sentence with a preposition' riposte; Quote Investigator finds the earliest 1942 version had no Churchill attribution and involved an anonymous schoolteacher.

candidates.quote: Our homes are our prisons; let us find freedom in their decoration.
candidates.trueOrigin: From the 1938 Chanel-credited Vogue maxims; possibly derived from or co-written by Pierre Reverdy.
candidates.whyNotable: A design-blog favorite attributed to Chanel; QI ties it to the same 1938 Vogue maxims collection that poet Pierre Reverdy may have authored, so Chanel's sole authorship is unconfirmed.

candidates.quote: The only beautiful eyes are those that look at us tenderly.
candidates.trueOrigin: Published under Chanel's name in Paris Vogue, September 1938, but the maxims may have been ghost-composed by poet Pierre Reverdy.
candidates.whyNotable: A romantic line shared as pure Chanel; QI confirms it appeared in Chanel's September 1938 Vogue maxims but notes a biography suggests poet Pierre Reverdy may have actually composed the maxims, clouding authorship.

candidates.quote: Always do sober what you said you'd do drunk. That will teach you to keep your mouth shut.
candidates.trueOrigin: QI found substantive evidence this originated with Hemingway (in a 1950s letter to publisher Charles Scribner IV), first published by Malcolm Forbes in 1961 — though the precise wording is uncertain and it is frequently conflated with the fabricated 'Write drunk, edit sober.'
candidates.whyNotable: Credibly Hemingway per QI, yet constantly garbled into the fake 'write drunk, edit sober' — a useful page to disambiguate the two.

candidates.quote: The first draft of anything is shit.
candidates.trueOrigin: First published in Arnold Samuelson's 1984 posthumous memoir 'With Hemingway,' recounting a 1930s conversation; no contemporaneous documentation exists, so the exact wording is unverified.
candidates.whyNotable: The go-to writing-advice quote; QI can only trace it to a student's memoir published 23 years after Hemingway's death.

candidates.quote: The most painful thing is losing yourself in the process of loving someone too much, and forgetting that you are special too.
candidates.trueOrigin: Often cited to 'Men Without Women' but appears nowhere in it; Wikiquote traces it to a 2011 blog post by Marc Chernoff, '30 Things to Stop Doing to Yourself.'
