candidates.trueOrigin: The Dalai Lama, 'The Art of Happiness' / compassion writings (cited via A Small Drop of Ink, 2003).
candidates.whyNotable: A genuine, frequently cited line with a sourced Wikiquote entry, useful as a verified hub anchor alongside the misattributions.

candidates.quote: My true religion is Kindness.
candidates.trueOrigin: The Dalai Lama, 'Kindness, Clarity, and Insight' (1984).
candidates.whyNotable: A genuine, widely quoted anchor line with a sourced Wikiquote entry from his book Kindness, Clarity, and Insight (1984).

candidates.quote: A person's a person, no matter how small.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely from Dr. Seuss, 'Horton Hears a Who!' (1954).
candidates.whyNotable: A real, book-sourced Seuss line that anchors the hub alongside the debunks; from Horton Hears a Who! (1954).

candidates.quote: The more that you read, the more things you will know. The more that you learn, the more places you'll go.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely from Dr. Seuss, 'I Can Read With My Eyes Shut!' (1978).
candidates.whyNotable: A genuine, book-sourced Seuss literacy line that serves as a verified anchor; from I Can Read With My Eyes Shut! (1978).

candidates.quote: Do what you feel in your heart to be right, for you'll be criticized anyway.
candidates.trueOrigin: Attributed to Eleanor Roosevelt in Dale Carnegie's How to Stop Worrying and Start Living (1944); credibly hers but not traced to a first-person source document.
candidates.whyNotable: A widely shared Roosevelt line with a real documentary trail, credited to her in Dale Carnegie's How to Stop Worrying and Start Living (1944).

candidates.quote: It takes courage to love, but pain through love is the purifying fire which those who love generously know.
candidates.trueOrigin: Eleanor Roosevelt, My Day column, April 1, 1939.
candidates.whyNotable: A genuinely sourced Roosevelt line, cited by Wikiquote to her My Day newspaper column of April 1, 1939.

candidates.quote: You gain strength, courage, and confidence by every experience in which you really stop to look fear in the face.
candidates.trueOrigin: Eleanor Roosevelt, You Learn by Living (1960), pp. 29-30.
candidates.whyNotable: A genuinely Roosevelt line, sourced by Wikiquote to her 1960 book You Learn by Living, serving as a real anchor alongside the debunks.

candidates.quote: Ich bin ein Berliner.
candidates.trueOrigin: John F. Kennedy, speech at Rudolph Wilde Platz, West Berlin, 26 June 1963.
candidates.whyNotable: JFK's celebrated Cold War declaration of solidarity with West Berlin, delivered in 1963.

candidates.quote: I can think of no more stirring symbol of man's humanity to man than a fire engine.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Vonnegut — dialogue spoken by the character Winston Niles Rumfoord in the 1959 novel The Sirens of Titan; Vonnegut echoed it himself in 2001.
candidates.whyNotable: Frequently doubted as a real Vonnegut line, but QI confirms he wrote it in The Sirens of Titan — a verified quote whose provenance people question.

candidates.quote: Please accept our apologies. We were roaring drunk on petroleum.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Vonnegut — his message to future generations delivered at the Connecticut Forum in Hartford in February 2006.
candidates.whyNotable: A biting climate-era line QI confirms Vonnegut actually said at a 2006 public forum — a verified quote with a specific documented occasion.

candidates.quote: So it goes.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Vonnegut — the recurring refrain in Slaughterhouse-Five (1969), spoken after every mention of death.
candidates.whyNotable: Vonnegut's signature verified catchphrase, endlessly quoted — a strong real anchor for the hub.

candidates.quote: The arts are not a way to make a living. They are a very human way of making life more bearable.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Vonnegut — from his 2005 essay collection A Man Without a Country.
candidates.whyNotable: A widely shared inspirational line that QI confirms is authentically Vonnegut, sourced to A Man Without a Country.

candidates.quote: We are what we pretend to be, so we must be careful about what we pretend to be.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Vonnegut — from the introduction to his 1961 novel Mother Night.
candidates.whyNotable: One of Vonnegut's most-quoted real lines and a good verified anchor to sit alongside the debunks.

candidates.quote: I restore myself when I'm alone. A career is born in public — talent in privacy.
candidates.trueOrigin: Marilyn Monroe, quoted in Ms. magazine, August 1972, p. 40.
candidates.whyNotable: A genuine sourced Monroe line that Wikiquote cites to Ms. magazine (August 1972), useful as a real anchor alongside the debunks.

candidates.quote: It's not quite true that I had nothing on. I had the radio on.
candidates.trueOrigin: Marilyn Monroe; earliest documented version in Sheilah Graham's June 1952 column.
candidates.whyNotable: Her celebrated quip about posing nude for a calendar; QI credits it to Monroe, with the earliest version appearing in a June 1952 gossip column.

candidates.quote: That's the trouble, a sex symbol becomes a thing. I just hate to be a thing.
candidates.trueOrigin: Marilyn Monroe, LIFE magazine interview with Richard Meryman, August 1962.
candidates.whyNotable: A rare genuine, well-sourced Monroe line; QI documents it from her LIFE magazine interview with Richard Meryman published in August 1962, just before her death.

candidates.quote: Life's most persistent and urgent question is, 'What are you doing for others?'
candidates.trueOrigin: Martin Luther King Jr., 'Strength to Love' (1963).
candidates.whyNotable: A verified real King line QI confirms from the 'Three Dimensions of a Complete Life' sermon in 'Strength to Love' (1963); a solid genuine anchor for the hub.

candidates.quote: Of all the forms of inequality, injustice in health care is the most shocking and inhumane.
candidates.trueOrigin: Martin Luther King Jr., Medical Committee for Human Rights, Chicago, March 25, 1966 (original wording 'health'/'inhuman').
candidates.whyNotable: Genuine (King, March 1966 Chicago health conference) but the viral wording is subtly altered — he actually said 'injustice in health is the most shocking and the most inhuman' — a strong misquote fact-check angle.

candidates.quote: True peace is not merely the absence of tension; it is the presence of justice.
candidates.trueOrigin: Martin Luther King Jr. (used mid-1950s; appears in 'A Martin Luther King Treasury,' 1964).
candidates.whyNotable: QI credits King with this formulation (used ~1954-55, published 1964), though earlier thematic precursors existed; a verified anchor line.

candidates.quote: I believe talent is like electricity. We don't understand electricity. We use it.
candidates.trueOrigin: Maya Angelou, 1983 interview with Claudia Tate.
candidates.whyNotable: A genuine Angelou line from her 1983 interview with Claudia Tate, verified by QI.

candidates.quote: I did then what I knew how to do. Now that I know better, I do better.
candidates.trueOrigin: Maya Angelou, credited by Oprah Winfrey and documented in a 1995 Washington Post article.
candidates.whyNotable: Popularized by Oprah Winfrey, who credited it to her friend Angelou; QI (1995 Washington Post) supports Angelou as the source.

candidates.quote: There is nothing quite so tragic as a young cynic, because it means the person has gone from knowing nothing to believing nothing.
candidates.trueOrigin: Maya Angelou, 1988 PBS documentary Facing Evil (Bill Moyers).
candidates.whyNotable: A genuine Angelou statement QI traces to the March 28, 1988 PBS/Bill Moyers documentary Facing Evil; later reference works corrupted 'tragic' to 'pitiful'.

candidates.quote: Without courage, you can't practice any other virtue consistently.
candidates.trueOrigin: Maya Angelou, quoted in USA Today, March 5, 1988.
candidates.whyNotable: A genuine, sourced Angelou line from USA Today (March 5, 1988), a solid real anchor for the hub.

candidates.quote: You may encounter many defeats, but you must not be defeated.
candidates.trueOrigin: Maya Angelou, earliest documented in a 1970 Los Angeles Times interview.
candidates.whyNotable: A genuine, recurring Angelou line QI traces to a 1970 Los Angeles Times interview and her 1983 Claudia Tate interview; a real anchor amid the fakes.

candidates.quote: Don't look for big things, just do small things with great love. The smaller the thing, the greater must be our love.
candidates.trueOrigin: Mother Teresa, in 'Mother Teresa: Come Be My Light' (2007).
candidates.whyNotable: The verified source of the ubiquitous 'do small things with great love' meme; Wikiquote cites it to 'Mother Teresa: Come Be My Light' (2007), letting the page correct the many mangled paraphrases.

candidates.quote: The biggest disease today is not leprosy or tuberculosis, but rather the feeling of being unwanted.
candidates.trueOrigin: Mother Teresa, quoted in Malcolm Muggeridge, 'Something Beautiful for God' (1971).
candidates.whyNotable: A genuinely sourced Mother Teresa line that anchors the hub; Wikiquote cites it to Malcolm Muggeridge's 'Something Beautiful for God' (1971).

candidates.quote: No one is born hating another person because of the colour of his skin, or his background, or his religion. People must learn to hate, and if they can learn to hate, they can be taught to love.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Mandela; from his 1994 autobiography Long Walk to Freedom.
candidates.whyNotable: A verified, widely-shared Mandela passage with a clear book source; strong genuine anchor alongside the misattribution debunks.

candidates.quote: Computers are useless. They can only give you answers.
candidates.trueOrigin: Traces to a 1964 Paris Review interview by William Fifield, where Picasso said of calculating machines 'But they are useless. They can only give you answers.' The modern 'computers' wording was refined over 1967-1986.
candidates.whyNotable: One of Picasso's most-quoted lines that QI actually substantiates, sourcing it to a documented 1964 Paris Review interview even though the 'computers' wording was polished later.

candidates.quote: Real artists ship.
candidates.trueOrigin: Quote Investigator concludes Jobs both coined and popularized it, per Andy Hertzfeld's account of a January 1983 Macintosh team offsite ('Quotations from Chairman Jobs').
candidates.whyNotable: A rare case where the popular attribution holds — QI confirms Jobs likely originated this Silicon Valley mantra, making it a strong verified anchor.

candidates.quote: Your time is limited, so don't waste it living someone else's life.
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely said by Jobs in his Stanford University commencement address, June 12, 2005.
candidates.whyNotable: One of Jobs's most-quoted real lines, with a firm primary source, giving the hub a verified anchor alongside the debunks.

candidates.quote: I only hope that we never lose sight of one thing — that it was all started by a mouse.
candidates.trueOrigin: Walt Disney, from The Disneyland Story television program (27 October 1954).
candidates.whyNotable: One of Disney's most iconic genuine lines, documented from his 1954 Disneyland Story television program.

candidates.quote: We keep moving forward, opening new doors, and doing new things, because we're curious and curiosity keeps leading us down new paths.
candidates.trueOrigin: Walt Disney, as quoted in the ending credits of Meet the Robinsons (2007).
candidates.whyNotable: A widely-shared Disney quote with a real documented source in the closing credits of Meet the Robinsons.

candidates.quote: Democracy is the worst form of government, except for all those other forms that have been tried from time to time
candidates.trueOrigin: Spoken by Churchill, House of Commons, 11 Nov 1947, but flagged by him as an existing saying; originator unknown (QI).
candidates.whyNotable: Churchill genuinely said this in the House of Commons on 11 November 1947, but he prefaced it with 'it has been said,' and QI shows he was repeating an already-circulating saying rather than coining it.

candidates.quote: Never in the field of human conflict was so much owed by so many to so few
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Churchill's, House of Commons, 20 August 1940.
candidates.whyNotable: A genuine, documented WWII anchor from Churchill's 20 August 1940 Commons speech honoring RAF pilots in the Battle of Britain.

candidates.quote: We shall fight on the beaches, we shall fight on the landing grounds, we shall fight in the fields and in the streets, we shall fight in the hills; we shall never surrender
candidates.trueOrigin: Genuinely Churchill's, House of Commons, 4 June 1940.
candidates.whyNotable: A genuine, fully documented anchor from Churchill's 4 June 1940 speech to the House of Commons after Dunkirk — a real line to balance the debunks.

candidates.quote: A man who is his own lawyer has a fool for a client.
candidates.trueOrigin: A legal proverb predating Lincoln by centuries; QI finds versions in print long before his birth, with no evidence he coined it.
candidates.whyNotable: Routinely pinned on lawyer-Lincoln; QI shows the maxim is an old proverb he did not originate.

candidates.quote: Better to remain silent and be thought a fool than to speak and remove all doubt.
candidates.trueOrigin: No evidence from Lincoln or Twain; QI's earliest match is Maurice Switzer's 1907 book, echoing Proverbs 17:28. First tied to Lincoln in Golden Book magazine (Nov 1931).
candidates.whyNotable: One of the internet's most misattributed maxims, credited to both Lincoln and Twain; QI traces it to a 1907 humor book and the Book of Proverbs.

candidates.quote: Whatever you are, be a good one.
candidates.trueOrigin: Attributed to novelist William Makepeace Thackeray, who reportedly said 'Whatever you are, try to be a good one' (recorded in Laurence Hutton's 1897 memoir); the Lincoln attribution surfaced only decades after his death.
candidates.whyNotable: An enormously popular motivational line on posters and mugs; documented as Thackeray's, not Lincoln's.

candidates.quote: You cannot help the poor by destroying the rich. You cannot strengthen the weak by weakening the strong.
candidates.trueOrigin: The Rev. William J. H. Boetcker, from his 1916 pamphlet later known as 'The Ten Cannots'; a 1942 leaflet ('Lincoln on Limitations') printed genuine Lincoln lines alongside Boetcker's with the attributions swapped.
candidates.whyNotable: One of the most-shared fake Lincoln quotes; the pro-capitalism 'Ten Cannots' were repeated as Lincoln's by Reagan (1992 RNC) and George H.W. Bush before fact-checkers traced them to Boetcker.

candidates.quote: There is only one way to avoid criticism: do nothing, say nothing, and be nothing.
candidates.trueOrigin: Elbert Hubbard, Little Journeys to the Homes of American Statesmen (1898), p. 370
candidates.whyNotable: A hugely shared motivational line credited to Aristotle; both Wikiquote and Quote Investigator trace the earliest strong match to Elbert Hubbard (1898), not Aristotle.

candidates.quote: Those who can, do; those who cannot, teach.
candidates.trueOrigin: George Bernard Shaw, Man and Superman (1903)
candidates.whyNotable: Frequently mis-pinned on Aristotle; Wikiquote credits George Bernard Shaw's Man and Superman (1903): 'He who can, does. He who cannot, teaches.'

candidates.quote: We are what we repeatedly do. Excellence, then, is not an act, but a habit.
candidates.trueOrigin: Will Durant, The Story of Philosophy (1926), Ch. II, paraphrasing Nicomachean Ethics Book II.4 / Book I.7
candidates.whyNotable: One of the single most-shared 'Aristotle' quotes on the internet; Wikiquote traces the exact wording to Will Durant's 1926 The Story of Philosophy, where Durant was summarizing Aristotle rather than quoting him.

candidates.quote: The great tragedy of Science — the slaying of a beautiful hypothesis by an ugly fact.
candidates.trueOrigin: Thomas Henry Huxley, in an 1870 address to the British Association in Liverpool, published in Nature.
candidates.whyNotable: Popular scientific aphorism sometimes credited to Darwin (an 1901 newspaper gave him a variant); QI confirms it belongs to his ally Thomas Henry Huxley.

candidates.quote: Better a diamond with a flaw than a pebble without
candidates.trueOrigin: Ming Dynasty scholar Jiao Hong (1540-1620)
candidates.whyNotable: Popular 'wisdom' line credited to Confucius that Wikiquote reassigns to Ming scholar Jiao Hong.

candidates.quote: I hear and I forget. I see and I remember. I do and I understand
candidates.trueOrigin: Earliest partial match traced to Xunzi; no evidence Confucius (or Benjamin Franklin) said it
candidates.whyNotable: Ubiquitous 'active learning' maxim pinned on Confucius; QI and Wikiquote trace the earliest partial match to Xunzi.

candidates.quote: Our greatest glory is not in never falling, but in rising every time we fall
candidates.trueOrigin: Oliver Goldsmith (18th-century), whose fictional 'Chinese' letters led readers to think it was Confucian
candidates.whyNotable: A hugely popular resilience quote credited to Confucius; QI concludes Oliver Goldsmith crafted it.

candidates.quote: The journey of a thousand miles begins with a single step
candidates.trueOrigin: Laozi, Tao Te Ching, Chapter 64
candidates.whyNotable: One of the most-shared 'Confucius' lines online, but Wikiquote reassigns it to Laozi's Tao Te Ching.

candidates.quote: Sometimes you will never know the value of a moment until it becomes a memory.
candidates.trueOrigin: Attributed by Wikiquote to Georges Duhamel, 'The Heart's Domain' (1919); no basis in Seuss's work.
candidates.whyNotable: A widely reposted sentimental 'Seuss' line that Wikiquote reassigns to Georges Duhamel's 1919 book.

candidates.quote: Those who dance appear insane to those who cannot hear the music.
candidates.trueOrigin: No Nietzsche source located; a similar image appears in Germaine de Stael's 'On Germany' (1813) and it circulated as an 'old proverb' by the 1920s.
candidates.whyNotable: One of the most-shared fake Nietzsche lines; QI and Wikiquote find no Nietzsche source — the sentiment predates him as a 19th-century proverb.

candidates.quote: I do not believe in a fate that falls on men however they act; but I do believe in a fate that falls on them unless they act.
candidates.trueOrigin: Actually written by G. K. Chesterton in 'On Holland,' Illustrated London News (29 April 1922).
candidates.whyNotable: A 'fate' quote pinned on Buddha; Wikiquote reassigns it to G. K. Chesterton (1922).

candidates.quote: To understand everything is to forgive everything.
candidates.trueOrigin: Generally reported as a French proverb ('tout comprendre c'est tout pardonner'); attached to Buddha without sources as early as Farm Journal Vol. 34 (1910).
candidates.whyNotable: Common 'Buddha' aphorism on forgiveness; Wikiquote shows it is really a French proverb attached to Buddha with no source.

candidates.quote: A free people ought not only to be armed and disciplined, but they should have sufficient arms and ammunition to maintain a status of independence from any who might attempt to abuse them.
candidates.trueOrigin: Corruption of Washington's authentic First Annual Address (8 January 1790); the 'sufficient arms and ammunition to maintain a status of independence' continuation is a modern fabrication.
candidates.whyNotable: A doctored gun-rights favorite: Washington's genuine 1790 line ('A free people ought not only to be armed, but disciplined...') was corrupted with a fabricated tail about arms and ammunition, which Quote Investigator debunked.

candidates.quote: Associate yourself with men of good quality if you esteem your own reputation, for it is better to be alone than in bad company.
candidates.trueOrigin: Rule 56 of 'Rules of Civility & Decent Behaviour in Company and Conversation,' maxims composed by French Jesuits in the 1590s and copied by young Washington c. 1744 as a penmanship exercise.
candidates.whyNotable: Passed around as original Washington counsel, but it is Rule 56 of the 'Rules of Civility' he copied as a schoolboy from a 16th-century French Jesuit courtesy manual.

candidates.quote: Firearms stand next in importance to the Constitution itself. They are the American people's liberty teeth and keystone under independence.
candidates.trueOrigin: C. S. Wheatley, 'Older Ideas of Firearms,' Hunter-Trader-Trapper magazine, September 1926; misattributed to Washington and spread through 1970s-80s newspapers.
candidates.whyNotable: One of the most-circulated fake gun-rights quotes; Quote Investigator and Wikiquote both trace it to a 1926 opinion piece by C. S. Wheatley, not to any Washington address.

candidates.quote: Government is like fire, a dangerous servant and a fearful master.
candidates.trueOrigin: Metaphor traced by Quote Investigator to John Tillotson's 1682 sermon 'The Danger of Zeal Without Knowledge'; the Washington ascription (from 1902) is unsupported.
candidates.whyNotable: Widely shared as Washington wisdom, but Quote Investigator found no 18th/19th-century link to him and traced the 'servant/master' fire metaphor to a 1682 sermon by Archbishop John Tillotson.

candidates.quote: The government of the United States is not, in any sense, founded on the Christian religion.
candidates.trueOrigin: Article 11 of the Treaty of Tripoli (1796-97), written by U.S. Consul Joel Barlow; signed into force under John Adams, not authored by Washington.
candidates.whyNotable: Frequently cited in church-and-state debates as Washington's words, but it is Article 11 of the Treaty of Tripoli, drafted by Joel Barlow and ratified under President John Adams in 1797.

candidates.quote: The marvel of all history is the patience with which men and women submit to burdens unnecessarily laid upon them by their governments.
candidates.trueOrigin: U.S. Senator William Edgar Borah, quoted in The Reader's Digest, Vol. 8, Issue 2, 1929, p. 776 — not Washington.
candidates.whyNotable: Shared as founding-father wisdom about tyranny, but Wikiquote documents it was written by U.S. Senator William E. Borah and published in Reader's Digest in 1929.

candidates.quote: None are so old as those who have outlived enthusiasm.
candidates.trueOrigin: Unknown; first tied to Thoreau in Kate Sanborn's A Year of Sunshine (1886) with no citation to his writings
candidates.whyNotable: Frequently quoted as Thoreau but never found in his works; Wikiquote's earliest Thoreau attributions are late-19th-century quotation anthologies (1886, 1894).

candidates.quote: Truths and roses have thorns about them.
candidates.trueOrigin: Pre-existing proverb; printed in Joseph Dennie's The Port Folio (1809) and a 1811 Spanish textbook before Thoreau recorded it
candidates.whyNotable: Though Thoreau copied it into his 1838 journal, Wikiquote shows it was a proverb already in print before his birth (The Port Folio, 1809), so he did not originate it.

candidates.quote: My best friend is the one who brings out the best in me.
candidates.trueOrigin: Harris Weinstock (May 1914), per Wikiquote; misattributed to Ford by 1948.
candidates.whyNotable: Widely shared friendship quote pinned on Ford; Wikiquote documents it actually originated with Harris Weinstock in 1914 and was misattributed to Ford by 1948.

candidates.quote: If a man does not know to what port he is sailing, no wind is favorable.
candidates.trueOrigin: Seneca the Younger (Epistulae Morales), not Socrates. JFK quoted it in a 1960 Raleigh, NC speech crediting Socrates; Wikiquote and QI note the true source is Seneca.
candidates.whyNotable: JFK cited this to Socrates, but it derives from Seneca the Younger — a documented misattribution noted on Wikiquote.

candidates.quote: First they ignore you, then they laugh at you, then they fight you, then you win.
candidates.trueOrigin: Nicholas Klein, 1918 Amalgamated Clothing Workers of America convention address ('First they ignore you. Then they ridicule you. And then they attack you and want to burn you. And then they build monuments to you.')
candidates.whyNotable: One of the most-shared fake Gandhi lines; there is no record of Gandhi saying it and QI/Wikiquote trace the closest variant to a 1918 US trade-union address by Nicholas Klein.

candidates.quote: God has no religion.
candidates.trueOrigin: Pre-dates Gandhi; appears in Henry Whitney Bellows, Re-statements of Christian Doctrine (1867). Gandhi attribution dates from the 1980s.
candidates.whyNotable: A tidy interfaith aphorism credited to Gandhi, but Wikiquote documents it predating him — e.g. in Henry Whitney Bellows's sermons (1867) — with the Gandhi attribution only appearing in the 1980s.

candidates.quote: If you're going to be a bear, be a grizzly.
candidates.trueOrigin: Earliest instance is George Hyde Preston's short story 'An Inside Tip,' Cosmopolitan Magazine, June 1908 (used in a stock-market context); no Gandhi connection.
candidates.whyNotable: An implausibly aggressive line to pin on a pacifist; QI found no evidence Gandhi said it and traces the phrase to a 1908 Cosmopolitan short story.

candidates.quote: I would have written a shorter letter, but I did not have the time.
candidates.trueOrigin: Blaise Pascal, Lettres provinciales (1657): 'I have made this longer than usual because I have not had time to make it shorter.'
candidates.whyNotable: Widely pinned on Twain, but the line predates him — it's from Blaise Pascal's Lettres provinciales (1657).

candidates.quote: Everything that is done in the world is done by hope.
candidates.trueOrigin: Martin Luther, leader of the Protestant Reformation (16th century).
candidates.whyNotable: A classic namesake mix-up: Wikiquote attributes it to Martin Luther, the 16th-century Protestant Reformer, not Martin Luther King Jr.

candidates.quote: Hate destroys the hater.
candidates.trueOrigin: Anonymous proverb documented from at least 1897 (Henry Norman, A. P. Buchman); King used a fuller variant in 1957.
candidates.whyNotable: Popularly attributed to King, but QI shows the proverb circulated by the 1890s; King's actual line was 'hate destroys the hater as well as the hated' in his 1957 'Loving Your Enemies' sermon.

candidates.quote: Justice runs down like water, and righteousness like a mighty stream.
candidates.trueOrigin: Book of Amos 5:24 (Hebrew Bible); King quoted it in speeches.
candidates.whyNotable: Made famous by King's 'I Have a Dream' delivery, but the words are scripture — Amos 5:24 — which Wikiquote lists as the true source.

candidates.quote: The arc of the moral universe is long, but it bends toward justice.
candidates.trueOrigin: Theodore Parker, 'Ten Sermons of Religion' (1853); King popularized a condensed form starting 1958.
candidates.whyNotable: Iconic line universally pinned on King, but QI shows it was coined by abolitionist minister Theodore Parker in 1853; King quoted it (in quotation marks) rather than authoring it.

candidates.quote: I like work: it fascinates me. I can sit and look at it for hours.
candidates.trueOrigin: Jerome K. Jerome, Three Men in a Boat (1889).
candidates.whyNotable: Popular 'lazy' aphorism routinely pinned on Wilde; Wikiquote reassigns it to Jerome K. Jerome's Three Men in a Boat.

candidates.quote: I'm not young enough to know everything.
candidates.trueOrigin: J. M. Barrie, The Admirable Crichton (1903).
candidates.whyNotable: Widely credited to Wilde, but both Wikiquote and Quote Investigator assign it to J. M. Barrie's play The Admirable Crichton.

candidates.quote: Atheism is a disease of the soul, before it becomes an error of the understanding.
candidates.trueOrigin: William Fleming, as quoted in Samuel Austin Allibone's 'Prose Quotations from Socrates to Macaulay'; not Plato's words.
candidates.whyNotable: A frequently-cited 'Plato' line in religious debate; Wikiquote identifies the real author as 19th-century writer William Fleming.

candidates.quote: Be kind, for everyone you meet is fighting a hard battle.
candidates.trueOrigin: Scottish author Ian Maclaren (pen name of Rev. John Watson), c. 1897-1898; original phrasing used 'Be pitiful, for every man is fighting a hard battle.'
candidates.whyNotable: One of the most-shared feel-good lines pinned on Plato; both Wikiquote and QI trace it to a late-1890s Scottish preacher, ~2,400 years after Plato.

candidates.quote: Music is a moral law. It gives soul to the universe, wings to the mind, flight to the imagination, and charm and gaiety to life and to everything.
candidates.trueOrigin: Does not appear in Plato; first attributed to him in John Lubbock's 'The Pleasures of Life, Part II' (1889).
candidates.whyNotable: A beloved 'Plato' music quote plastered across posters and album notes; Wikiquote traces the attribution to an 1889 Lubbock book.

candidates.quote: Necessity is the mother of invention.
candidates.trueOrigin: An English proverb read into Benjamin Jowett's flowery Victorian translation of Republic II 369c; Plato's literal text is only 'our need will be the real creator.'
candidates.whyNotable: A ubiquitous proverb credited to Plato only via Jowett's loose translation; Wikiquote documents the literal Greek says no such thing.

candidates.quote: Only the dead have seen the end of war.
candidates.trueOrigin: George Santayana, 'Soliloquies in England' (1922); no source in Plato exists. Popularized as 'Plato' by a 1990s film and a Ridley Scott quote.
candidates.whyNotable: Famously misattributed to Plato (even carved as such at Imperial War Museum); Wikiquote flags the real author as Santayana.

candidates.quote: You can discover more about a person in an hour of play than in a year of conversation.
candidates.trueOrigin: Paraphrase of Richard Lingard's 1670 'A Letter of Advice to a Young Gentleman,' which read 'you will then learn more of him in one hour, than in seven years conversation.'
candidates.whyNotable: A hugely-shared 'Plato' line QI debunks, tracing it to a 1670 English advice pamphlet with no connection to Plato.

candidates.quote: The man who grasps principles can successfully select his own methods. The man who tries methods, ignoring principles, is sure to have trouble.
candidates.trueOrigin: Harrington Emerson, The Twelve Principles of Efficiency (1912)
candidates.whyNotable: A classic name-collision misattribution: QI shows it was written by efficiency engineer Harrington Emerson, whom the fame of Ralph Waldo Emerson eclipsed.

candidates.quote: To laugh often and much; to win the respect of intelligent people and the affection of children... to know even one life has breathed easier because you have lived. This is to have succeeded.
candidates.trueOrigin: Bessie Anderson Stanley, 'What is Success?' in Heart Throbs Volume Two (1911)
candidates.whyNotable: The ubiquitous 'What is Success?' poem pinned on Emerson across the internet; Wikiquote credits Bessie Anderson Stanley's 1911 essay in Heart Throbs, Volume Two.

candidates.quote: Know thyself.
candidates.trueOrigin: Delphic maxim (Temple of Apollo at Delphi); Seven Sages of Greece
candidates.whyNotable: Constantly attributed to Socrates but it is the Delphic maxim inscribed at the Temple of Apollo, traditionally ascribed to the Seven Sages (often Solon or Chilon) and predating Socrates.

candidates.quote: I sincerely believe that banking institutions are more dangerous to our liberties than standing armies.
candidates.trueOrigin: Paraphrase compiled from three separate Jefferson letters (1813-1817); the fused wording first appears in 1895
candidates.whyNotable: Widely shared as a clean Jefferson quote, but Wikiquote shows the popular one-liner is a stitched paraphrase of three separate Jefferson letters (1813-1817), first appearing in this form in 1895.

candidates.quote: The best government is that which governs least.
candidates.trueOrigin: Motto of the United States Magazine and Democratic Review (1837); later quoted by Henry David Thoreau
candidates.whyNotable: A small-government slogan routinely credited to Jefferson; Wikiquote shows it as the 1837 motto of the United States Magazine and Democratic Review, later used by Thoreau, with no Jefferson source.

candidates.quote: The price of freedom is eternal vigilance.
candidates.trueOrigin: John Philpot Curran, 1790 speech ("The Right of Election of the Lord Mayor of Dublin")
candidates.whyNotable: Constantly attributed to Jefferson but never found in his writings; Wikiquote traces the phrasing to John Philpot Curran's 1790 speech on the right of election.

candidates.quote: When governments fear the people, there is liberty. When the people fear the government, there is tyranny.
candidates.trueOrigin: John Basil Barnhill, in a 1914 published debate (Barnhill vs. Tichenor)
candidates.whyNotable: One of the most-shared fake Jefferson lines on freedom; Wikiquote traces it to John Basil Barnhill's 1914 socialist debate writings, first pinned on Jefferson only in 1945.

candidates.quote: Anything that is too stupid to be spoken is sung
candidates.trueOrigin: Pierre de Beaumarchais, Le Barbier de Seville (1775)
candidates.whyNotable: Widely pinned on Voltaire but Wikiquote traces it to Beaumarchais's Le Barbier de Seville (1775): 'what isn't worth saying is sung.'

candidates.quote: I disapprove of what you say, but I will defend to the death your right to say it
candidates.trueOrigin: Evelyn Beatrice Hall (pen name S. G. Tallentyre), The Friends of Voltaire (1906)
candidates.whyNotable: The single most-cited fake Voltaire line; both Wikiquote and QI trace it to biographer Evelyn Beatrice Hall, who coined it in 1906 as a summary of Voltaire's attitude, not a real quote.

candidates.quote: Judge a man by his questions rather than by his answers
candidates.trueOrigin: Pierre-Marc-Gaston, duc de Levis, Maximes et reflexions (1808)
candidates.whyNotable: A popular inspirational line credited to Voltaire that Wikiquote reassigns to the duc de Levis's 1808 Maximes et reflexions.

candidates.quote: Nothing can be more contrary to religion and the clergy than reason and common sense
candidates.trueOrigin: Paul-Henri Thiry, Baron d'Holbach, Theologie portative (1768)
candidates.whyNotable: A frequently shared anti-clerical zinger that Wikiquote attributes instead to Baron d'Holbach's Theologie portative (1768).

candidates.quote: You have enemies? Good. That means you've stood up for something, sometime in your life
candidates.trueOrigin: Victor Hugo, 'Villemain' (1845), from his journal Choses Vues.
candidates.whyNotable: A hugely shared empowerment quote that is actually Victor Hugo's, from his 1845 essay 'Villemain' in Choses Vues.

candidates.quote: Folks are usually about as happy as they make up their minds to be.
candidates.trueOrigin: No substantive evidence Lincoln used the expression; QI's earliest matches are 20th-century and unconnected to Lincoln.
candidates.whyNotable: A ubiquitous feel-good line pinned on Lincoln across social media; QI found no support for the attribution.

candidates.quote: Give me six hours to chop down a tree and I will spend the first four sharpening the axe.
candidates.trueOrigin: No evidence Lincoln said it; QI finds the 'sharpen the axe' preparation proverb only much later and unlinked to Lincoln.
candidates.whyNotable: A staple of productivity and leadership decks; QI shows the vivid Lincoln version has no 19th-century basis.

candidates.quote: I destroy my enemies when I make them my friends.
candidates.trueOrigin: No substantive evidence Lincoln said it; QI traces the sentiment to much earlier sources with no Lincoln connection.
candidates.whyNotable: Widely shared as Lincoln wisdom (and quoted in speeches); QI found no contemporaneous evidence tying it to him.

candidates.quote: Compound interest is the eighth wonder of the world. He who understands it, earns it; he who doesn't, pays it
candidates.trueOrigin: Anonymous advertising copy (1920s bank ads); Einstein attribution first appears 1988.
candidates.whyNotable: The finance world's favorite fake Einstein line; QI finds no evidence Einstein, Rothschild, or Rockefeller ever said it and traces the 'eighth wonder' label for compound interest to anonymous 1920s bank advertising, first pinned on Einstein by a financial analyst in 1988.

candidates.quote: Everybody is a genius. But if you judge a fish by its ability to climb a tree, it will live its whole life believing that it is stupid
candidates.trueOrigin: Unknown; earliest attribution ~2004 self-help writing, allegory predates Einstein by decades.
candidates.whyNotable: A viral education/self-esteem meme; QI finds no Einstein source and traces the earliest close match to ~2004 (Matthew Kelly's self-help book 'The Rhythm of Life'), with the fish-and-tree allegory circulating among educators for over a century.

candidates.quote: If the bee disappeared off the surface of the globe, man would have only four years left to live
candidates.trueOrigin: Anonymous; earliest appearance a 1994 beekeepers' protest pamphlet in Brussels.
candidates.whyNotable: An environmentalist rallying cry falsely credited to Einstein; Snopes finds no such statement in any Einstein compilation and traces it to a 1994 Brussels beekeepers' protest pamphlet, listed under 'Probably not by Einstein' in The Ultimate Quotable Einstein.

candidates.quote: If you can't explain it simply, you don't understand it well enough
candidates.trueOrigin: Unknown; no Einstein source, commonly reassigned to Richard Feynman or Ernest Rutherford without evidence.
candidates.whyNotable: A staple of teaching and startup slide decks; listed among Einstein's misattributed quotes with no evidence he said it, and often traced instead to later figures like Feynman or Rutherford.

candidates.quote: Courage is rightly esteemed the first of human qualities because it is the quality which guarantees all others.
candidates.trueOrigin: Popularized by Winston Churchill (1931); not from Aristotle
candidates.whyNotable: Often attributed to Aristotle in leadership circles; Quote Investigator finds the ascription unsupported, with the phrasing tied to Winston Churchill (1931) and later writers.

candidates.quote: Tell 'em what you're going to tell 'em; next, tell 'em; next, tell 'em what you told 'em.
candidates.trueOrigin: 20th-century public-speaking lore; not traceable to Aristotle
candidates.whyNotable: A public-speaking maxim routinely credited to Aristotle's Rhetoric; Quote Investigator finds the ascription unsupported and points to 20th-century speech instructors.

candidates.quote: The place where your talent meets the world's needs is the job God has in mind for you.
candidates.trueOrigin: 20th-century origin (linked to Marcus Bach / Albert Schweitzer paraphrases); not Aristotle
candidates.whyNotable: A viral 'find your calling' quote credited to Aristotle; Quote Investigator finds no support for the Aristotle ascription and points to 20th-century sources like Marcus Bach.

candidates.quote: The worst form of inequality is to try to make unequal things equal.
candidates.trueOrigin: Condensed by Laurence J. Peter (Peter's People, 1979); loose gloss on Politics III.V.8
candidates.whyNotable: A political-meme staple; Wikiquote traces the condensed 'Aristotle's Axiom' wording to Laurence J. Peter's 1979 Peter's People via a 1916 Treitschke translation, only loosely based on Politics III.V.8.

candidates.quote: Tolerance and apathy are the last virtues of a dying society.
candidates.trueOrigin: No known source; not in any extant Aristotle work
candidates.whyNotable: A viral culture-war line pinned on Aristotle; Wikiquote states it is not found in any extant work of Aristotle.

candidates.quote: Anyone who doesn't believe in miracles is not a realist.
candidates.trueOrigin: David Ben-Gurion, first Prime Minister of Israel, as cited in "Psychosocial Care of the Dying Patient" (1978); Wikiquote reassigns it to him.
candidates.whyNotable: Commonly circulated as a Hepburn line; Wikiquote reassigns it to David Ben-Gurion.

candidates.quote: Happy girls are the prettiest.
candidates.trueOrigin: A fragment of the post-2007 "I believe in pink" internet passage that Wikiquote lists as misattributed; no lifetime Hepburn source exists.
candidates.whyNotable: Heavily shared as a standalone Hepburn line, but it is lifted from the same fabricated "I believe in pink" passage Wikiquote debunks.

candidates.quote: I believe in pink. I believe that laughing is the best calorie burner. I believe in kissing, kissing a lot. I believe in being strong when everything seems to be going wrong. I believe that happy girls are the prettiest girls. I believe that tomorrow is another day and I believe in miracles.
candidates.trueOrigin: No evidence Hepburn ever said or wrote it; Wikiquote traces the earliest documented appearance to an unidentified MySpace member circa 2007-08, well after her 1993 death, before it was pinned on her in outlets like Glamour (2012).
candidates.whyNotable: A wildly viral feel-good "I believe in pink" passage; Wikiquote flags it as a post-2007 internet fabrication with no lifetime source.

candidates.quote: Beer is proof that God loves us and wants us to be happy
candidates.trueOrigin: A misquotation of Franklin's real 1779 letter to Andre Morellet, which praised wine (not beer) as 'a constant proof that God loves us, and loves to see us happy.'
candidates.whyNotable: One of the most-shared fake Franklin lines on beer coasters and merch; Wikiquote and QI show Franklin actually wrote it about WINE, not beer, in a 1779 letter to the Abbe Morellet.

candidates.quote: By failing to prepare, you are preparing to fail
candidates.trueOrigin: No evidence Franklin said or wrote it in any form.
candidates.whyNotable: An extremely common productivity/motivational quote credited to Franklin; Wikiquote finds no evidence he coined any form of it.

candidates.quote: Democracy is two wolves and a lamb voting on what to have for lunch
candidates.trueOrigin: Not found in Franklin's works; earliest documented uses date to circa 1990 (Gary Strand) and 1992 (Marvin Simkin).
candidates.whyNotable: A staple of libertarian social-media posts falsely branded as Franklin; Wikiquote finds nothing in his writings, with earliest known instances from Usenet-era authors Gary Strand (1990) and Marvin Simkin (1992).

candidates.quote: Tell me and I forget. Teach me and I may remember. Involve me and I learn.
candidates.trueOrigin: No evidence Franklin wrote it; the idea traces to far older proverbs (often linked to the Chinese Xunzi), with the modern three-part wording emerging in the 20th century.
candidates.whyNotable: Ubiquitous classroom-poster quote credited to Franklin; QI finds no substantive evidence he crafted it, with the sentiment echoing much older proverbs including the Chinese Xunzi.

candidates.quote: The definition of insanity is doing the same thing over and over again and expecting different results
candidates.trueOrigin: No evidence Franklin said it; earliest documented forms appear in a 1981 Narcotics Anonymous pamphlet, with an earlier variant from Osho (1975).
candidates.whyNotable: A viral motivational meme pinned interchangeably on Franklin, Einstein, and Twain; Wikiquote finds no evidence for any of them, tracing it to a 1981 Narcotics Anonymous text and an earlier 1975 Osho variant.

candidates.quote: We do not stop playing because we grow old; we grow old because we stop playing
candidates.trueOrigin: An anonymous modern rewording of a statement by psychologist G. Stanley Hall in Adolescence (1904); not Franklin's.
candidates.whyNotable: A feel-good aging quote widely attributed to Franklin (and George Bernard Shaw); Wikiquote identifies it as an anonymous modern variant of a line from G. Stanley Hall's 1904 'Adolescence.'

candidates.quote: When the people find that they can vote themselves money, that will herald the end of the republic
candidates.trueOrigin: Unsourced; the same sentiment is separately misattributed to Alexis de Tocqueville and Alexander Fraser Tytler, with no evidence for Franklin.
candidates.whyNotable: A popular political-warning quote pinned on Franklin (and also on Tocqueville and Tytler); Wikiquote finds no evidence any of them wrote it.

candidates.quote: A mathematician is a blind man in a dark room looking for a black cat which isn't there.
candidates.trueOrigin: Earlier variants (using a 'black hat') attributed to Lord Bowen and William James; no evidence Darwin ever said it.
candidates.whyNotable: A stock joke about mathematicians (and metaphysicians) falsely pinned on Darwin; QI and Wikiquote trace earlier 'black hat' variants to Lord Bowen and William James.

candidates.quote: I was a young man with uninformed ideas. I threw out queries, suggestions, wondering all the time over everything; and to my astonishment the ideas took like wildfire. People made a religion of them.
candidates.trueOrigin: Invented by the evangelist 'Lady Hope' in a 1915 account; refuted by Darwin's family, who confirmed she was never present during his final illness.
candidates.whyNotable: The centerpiece of the fabricated 'Lady Hope' deathbed-recantation story in which Darwin supposedly disavowed evolution; his daughter Henrietta stated the whole tale 'has no foundation whatever.'

candidates.quote: In the struggle for survival, the fittest win out at the expense of their rivals because they succeed in adapting themselves best to their environment.
candidates.trueOrigin: A summary sentence written by textbook authors Wallbank, Taylor and Bailkey in the 1940s history text 'Civilization Past and Present,' not Darwin's own words.
candidates.whyNotable: Circulated for decades as a line from On the Origin of Species; the Darwin Correspondence Project lists it among 'six things Darwin never said.'

candidates.quote: It is not the strongest of the species that survives, nor the most intelligent that survives. It is the one that is most adaptable to change.
candidates.trueOrigin: A 1963 paraphrase of Darwin's ideas by Louisiana State University business professor Leon C. Megginson, later hardened into a fake direct quotation; also misattributed to Clarence Darrow.
candidates.whyNotable: One of the most-shared fake Darwin quotes, plastered on corporate slides and motivational posters; QI and the Darwin Correspondence Project confirm Darwin never wrote it.

candidates.quote: The Creator has an inordinate fondness for beetles.
candidates.trueOrigin: Most likely J.B.S. Haldane (exact wording apocryphal; earliest documented version 1959 calls it 'possibly apocryphal'), not Darwin.
candidates.whyNotable: A witty line about the abundance of beetle species frequently pinned on Darwin the famous beetle collector; QI traces it instead to geneticist J.B.S. Haldane.

candidates.quote: A picture is worth a thousand words
candidates.trueOrigin: Not Chinese; popularized by advertising man Fred R. Barnard in the 1920s, later dressed up as a Chinese proverb
candidates.whyNotable: Often billed as an ancient Chinese/Confucius proverb; QI shows the 'Chinese origin' claim is late, weak, and a 1920s ad-man invention.

candidates.quote: The best time to plant a tree was 20 years ago. The second best time is now
candidates.trueOrigin: Anonymous American saying; QI finds no evidence it is a Chinese proverb, earliest use 1967
candidates.whyNotable: Endlessly labeled a Confucius/Chinese proverb, but QI finds the creator anonymous and the Chinese attribution weak and late.

candidates.quote: Be who you are and say what you feel, because those who mind don't matter and those who matter don't mind.
candidates.trueOrigin: The 'those who mind don't matter' half traces to Bernard Baruch (popularized 1948) and appears in print as anonymous wisdom as early as 1938; the combined feel-good version pinned on Seuss has no citation in his work.
candidates.whyNotable: A ubiquitous 'be yourself' Seuss meme; QI shows the core saying predates Seuss and belongs to Bernard Baruch, with no evidence Seuss ever wrote the combined line.

candidates.quote: You know you're in love when you can't fall asleep because reality is finally better than your dreams.
candidates.trueOrigin: Circulates on social media credited to Seuss with no citation; not found in any Seuss work. Origin unknown.
candidates.whyNotable: A perennial romantic-caption fake Seuss line flagged by Wikiquote as attributed to him with no source.

candidates.quote: Great minds discuss ideas; average minds discuss events; small minds discuss people.
candidates.trueOrigin: Precursors predate Roosevelt; the tiered form is linked in QI's analysis to a lineage associated with historian Henry Thomas Buckle (1821-1862), not Eleanor Roosevelt.
candidates.whyNotable: A hugely popular tiered aphorism pinned on Roosevelt, but QI and Wikiquote trace its lineage to earlier sources (associated with historian Henry Thomas Buckle), not to her.

candidates.quote: You wouldn't worry so much about what other people think of you if you realized how seldom they do.
candidates.trueOrigin: Olin Miller, a professional humorist, identified by QI as the most likely originator.
candidates.whyNotable: Widely attributed to Roosevelt, but QI traces the remark to jokesmith Olin Miller, whom it names as the most likely originator.

candidates.quote: Most people are not seeking truth; they are searching for comfort in illusions.
candidates.trueOrigin: No source in Nietzsche located; origin unknown, likely a modern paraphrase.
candidates.whyNotable: A popular quote-card line flagged by Wikiquote as misattributed with no located source in Nietzsche's works.

candidates.quote: Nobody is more inferior than those who insist on being equal.
candidates.trueOrigin: No genuine Nietzsche source; earliest verifiable appearance is a fictional 'mock interview' by Richard Marshall.
candidates.whyNotable: Frequently shared on social media as Nietzsche; Wikiquote finds the only traceable source is a mock/satirical interview, not Nietzsche.

candidates.quote: They muddy the waters to make them look deep.
candidates.trueOrigin: Attributed to Nietzsche in Robert C. Solomon's 'Spirituality for the Skeptic' (2002) with no specific source given.
candidates.whyNotable: A punchy line often credited to Nietzsche; Wikiquote traces the attribution to Robert C. Solomon's 2002 book with no primary Nietzsche source.

candidates.quote: Believe nothing, no matter where you read it or who has said it, not even if I have said it, unless it agrees with your own reason and your own common sense.
candidates.trueOrigin: A distorted paraphrase that actually contradicts the Kalama Sutta it is drawn from; Wikiquote flags it as a bad/spurious translation with no canonical basis.
candidates.whyNotable: The famous 'believe nothing... unless it agrees with your reason' quote; Wikiquote shows it is a corrupted rendering that inverts the actual Kalama Sutta.

candidates.quote: Government is not reason, it is not eloquence, it is force; like fire, a troublesome servant and a fearful master.
candidates.trueOrigin: Apocryphal; earliest documented appearance in The Christian Science Journal (1902), unattributed and undocumented.
candidates.whyNotable: A staple of anti-government and libertarian memes routinely pinned on Washington's Farewell Address; it appears in no Washington writing and first surfaced in the Christian Science Journal in 1902, over a century after his death.

candidates.quote: I cannot tell a lie, I did it with my little hatchet.
candidates.trueOrigin: Fabricated anecdote from Mason Locke (Parson) Weems, 'The Life of Washington' (1806 edition); the cherry-tree story has no basis in fact.
candidates.whyNotable: The single most famous George Washington 'quote' in American culture; the cherry-tree confession was invented whole-cloth by biographer Parson Weems in the 1806 edition of his Washington hagiography.

candidates.quote: It is impossible to rightly govern the world without God and the Bible.
candidates.trueOrigin: Evolved fabrication first traced to an undocumented 1830s biography, progressively reworded in later-19th-century religious publications; not in any authentic Washington text.
candidates.whyNotable: A perennial in 'America was founded as a Christian nation' arguments; Wikiquote shows it is a fabrication that evolved through undocumented 19th-century biographies and appears nowhere in Washington's writings or Farewell Address.

candidates.quote: Happiness is like a butterfly: the more you chase it, the more it will elude you, but if you turn your attention to other things, it will come and sit softly on your shoulder.
candidates.trueOrigin: Butterfly-of-happiness metaphor traced by QI to an 1848 New Orleans Daily Crescent item signed 'L'; the modern wording has no Thoreau basis
candidates.whyNotable: A hugely popular feel-good quote pinned on Thoreau; Quote Investigator finds the butterfly metaphor circulating by 1848 and no support for a Thoreau attribution.

candidates.quote: Most men lead lives of quiet desperation and go to the grave with the song still in them.
candidates.trueOrigin: Corruption of Thoreau's Walden line 'The mass of men lead lives of quiet desperation'; the appended clause has no Thoreau source
candidates.whyNotable: A viral misquotation that welds a spurious 'song still in them' ending onto Thoreau's genuine Walden line; Wikiquote flags the added tail as unsourced.

candidates.quote: Success usually comes to those who are too busy to be looking for it.
candidates.trueOrigin: Earliest known appearance uncredited in Locomotive Engineers Journal, Vol. 76 (1942); no Thoreau source
candidates.whyNotable: A common motivational-poster quote assigned to Thoreau; Wikiquote's earliest sighting is an uncredited 1942 Locomotive Engineers Journal, with no Thoreau source.

candidates.quote: Wealth is the ability to fully experience life.
candidates.trueOrigin: No documented source in Thoreau's works; origin unknown
candidates.whyNotable: A popular social-media 'Thoreau' aphorism with no documented source in any of his writings, per Wikiquote's Misattributed section.

candidates.quote: If I had asked people what they wanted, they would have said faster horses.
candidates.trueOrigin: No credible source; not found in Ford's writings or interviews. Sentiment is a 20th-century paraphrase, first tied to Ford decades after his death.
candidates.whyNotable: One of the most-shared fake business/innovation quotes on the internet; QI finds no evidence Ford ever said it, with the earliest Ford linkage only in a 1999 cruise-industry newsletter, and HBR examined it in 2011.

candidates.quote: Stopping advertising to save money is like stopping your watch to save time.
candidates.trueOrigin: Unknown; predates its Ford attribution and has no source in Ford's writings.
candidates.whyNotable: A staple of marketing decks credited to Ford; Wikiquote flags it as misattributed, with Ford linkage appearing only about a decade after the saying itself circulated.

candidates.quote: A child miseducated is a child lost.
candidates.trueOrigin: Earliest documented use is a 2013 speech by Nigerian governor Umaru Tanko Al-Makura; no JFK source exists.
candidates.whyNotable: Circulated widely as a JFK line on education, but Wikiquote finds the earliest documented use is a 2013 Nigerian political speech.

candidates.quote: It is better to light a candle than to curse the darkness.
candidates.trueOrigin: A Christian proverb popularized by William L. Watkinson (1907); also widely tied to Eleanor Roosevelt. Not original to JFK.
candidates.whyNotable: A proverb pinned on many figures including JFK; QI traces it to a 1907 sermon by William L. Watkinson.

candidates.quote: The hottest places in Hell are reserved for those who in a period of moral crisis maintain their neutrality.
candidates.trueOrigin: Not found in Dante's works. A modern paraphrase JFK repeatedly popularized in 1950s-60s speeches while falsely crediting Dante; QI finds no matching passage in the Inferno.
candidates.whyNotable: JFK quoted this as Dante many times, but QI shows it appears nowhere in Dante — a modern paraphrase JFK helped cement in popular culture.

candidates.quote: The only thing necessary for the triumph of evil is that good men do nothing.
candidates.trueOrigin: Not found in Edmund Burke's writings. JFK cited it to Burke (e.g. before the Canadian Parliament, 1961), but QI finds no such line in Burke; it is an unverified modern construction.
candidates.whyNotable: JFK attributed this to Edmund Burke, but QI's classic investigation finds no such statement anywhere in Burke's works.

candidates.quote: There's a plot in this country to enslave every man, woman, and child. Before I leave this high and noble office, I intend to expose this plot.
candidates.trueOrigin: Fabricated. No such statement exists in the JFK record; the supposed 'seven days before his assassination' framing is invented. Debunked by Metabunk and fact-checked by Snopes.
candidates.whyNotable: A staple fabricated JFK quote in conspiracy circles, flagged as fake on Wikiquote and fact-checked false by Snopes and Metabunk.

candidates.quote: When everybody thinks alike, nobody will think at all.
candidates.trueOrigin: Uncertain. QI finds the aphorism variously credited to Walter Lippmann, George Patton, and Benjamin Franklin, with no solid link to JFK.
candidates.whyNotable: A groupthink aphorism attributed to JFK, Patton, and Franklin alike; QI finds no genuine JFK connection and earlier ties to Walter Lippmann.

candidates.quote: A patient is the most important person in our hospital. He is not an interruption to our work, he is the purpose of it.
candidates.trueOrigin: Anonymous customer-service/business slogan traceable to 1940s publications ('A customer is the most important visitor on our premises...'); attributed to Gandhi only since the 1970s.
candidates.whyNotable: Displayed as a 'Gandhi' motto in hospitals and businesses worldwide, but QI shows it derives from 1940s business/customer-service copy and was only attributed to Gandhi from the 1970s (he never ran a hospital).

candidates.quote: An eye for an eye will make the whole world blind.
candidates.trueOrigin: No Gandhi source located; antecedents include a 1914 Canadian House of Commons debate (George Perry Graham) and Louis Fischer's 1950 biography paraphrase; the exact popular wording is from John Briley's screenplay for the film Gandhi (1982).
candidates.whyNotable: A staple anti-violence meme credited to Gandhi; QI found no instance in his works, and the pithy wording was written for the 1982 film Gandhi by screenwriter John Briley.

candidates.quote: Be the change you wish to see in the world.
candidates.trueOrigin: Arleen Lorrance, 'The Love Project' (Brooklyn, 1974): 'be the change you want to see happen'; the Gandhi phrasing is first seen attributed to him in a 1987 New Mexico newspaper.
candidates.whyNotable: Probably the single most-pinned fake Gandhi line; QI and the NYT find no reliable documentary evidence in the 98-volume Collected Works, and the modern phrasing traces to educator Arleen Lorrance's 'Love Project' (1970s).

candidates.quote: A sex symbol is a heavy load to carry when one is tired, hurt and bewildered.
candidates.trueOrigin: Clara Bow, not Marilyn Monroe.
candidates.whyNotable: Frequently attributed to Monroe but Wikiquote documents it was actually spoken by silent-film star Clara Bow, the original 'It Girl'.

candidates.quote: A woman knows by intuition, or instinct, what is best for herself.
candidates.trueOrigin: Unknown; no documented source or connection to Monroe.
candidates.whyNotable: Circulates widely as Monroe wisdom on social media and in self-help literature, but Wikiquote lists it as unknown origin and date with no tie to her.

candidates.quote: I'm selfish, impatient and a little insecure. I make mistakes, I am out of control and at times hard to handle. But if you can't handle me at my worst, then you sure as hell don't deserve me at my best.
candidates.trueOrigin: Unknown; no documented source, first surfaced in internet/self-help circulation with no tie to Monroe's lifetime.
candidates.whyNotable: One of the single most-shared fake Monroe quotes on social media and self-help books; Wikiquote flags it as unknown origin with no source predating its viral spread.

candidates.quote: To all the girls that think you're fat because you're not a size zero, you're the beautiful one. It's society who's ugly.
candidates.trueOrigin: Unknown; anachronistic modern internet composition, no tie to Monroe.
candidates.whyNotable: A viral body-positivity line pinned on Monroe that references 'size zero,' a modern clothing-size concept that did not exist in her lifetime; Wikiquote flags it as unknown origin.

candidates.quote: Golf is a good walk spoiled.
candidates.trueOrigin: No genuine Twain source; earliest similar wording credited by H. S. Scrivener (1903) to 'the Allens', not Twain.
candidates.whyNotable: One of the most-repeated 'Twain' one-liners; Wikiquote finds no evidence he said it and traces a similar 1903 line to H. S. Scrivener crediting 'the Allens'.

candidates.quote: History doesn't repeat itself, but it often rhymes.
candidates.trueOrigin: No Twain source; the phrasing surfaces circa 1970 and cannot be traced to him.
candidates.whyNotable: An extremely viral aphorism attached to Twain; Wikiquote notes the wording first appears around 1970 with no evidence Twain wrote it.

candidates.quote: If voting made any difference, they wouldn't let us do it.
candidates.trueOrigin: No Twain source; similar sentiments credited to Philip Berrigan and Emma Goldman.
candidates.whyNotable: A perennial election-season 'Twain' quote; Wikiquote attributes the sentiment to Philip Berrigan and Emma Goldman, not Twain.

candidates.quote: If you don't read the newspaper, you are uninformed. If you do read the newspaper, you are misinformed.
candidates.trueOrigin: No Twain source; modern wording is not traceable to him per Quote Investigator.
candidates.whyNotable: A media-distrust favorite; Quote Investigator finds no substantive evidence Twain said it, with the modern phrasing emerging long after his death.

candidates.quote: It's not the size of the dog in the fight, it's the size of the fight in the dog.
candidates.trueOrigin: American proverb; earliest known version from Arthur G. Lewis (1911), not Twain.
candidates.whyNotable: A motivational-poster staple credited to Twain online since 1998; Wikiquote finds no contemporary evidence and traces an early version to Arthur G. Lewis (1911).

candidates.quote: The coldest winter I ever spent was a summer in San Francisco.
candidates.trueOrigin: Origin unknown; not found in Twain's writings. Twain described SF weather differently in Roughing It.
candidates.whyNotable: A San Francisco tourism cliche pinned on Twain everywhere; Quote Investigator and Wikiquote find no match in his papers or speeches.

candidates.quote: When I was a boy of fourteen, my father was so ignorant I could hardly stand to have the old man around. But when I got to be twenty-one, I was astonished at how much the old man had learned in seven years.
candidates.trueOrigin: No genuine Twain source located; apocryphal per Quote Investigator.
candidates.whyNotable: A viral 'growing up' quip; Quote Investigator rates it a probable misattribution with no support in Twain's works.

candidates.quote: Since the dawn of history the negro has owned the continent of Africa, rich beyond the dream of poet's fancy, crunching acres of diamonds beneath his bare black feet.
candidates.trueOrigin: Thomas Dixon Jr.'s 1905 novel 'The Clansman,' where the words are spoken by a character; never written by Darwin.
candidates.whyNotable: A racist passage circulated online as proof of Darwin's bigotry; Wikiquote documents that it is not Darwin at all but lifted from a 1905 novel — a high-value debunk that clears a fabricated attribution.
